page: Vultr vx1-m-48c-384g-2880s is a memory-optimized server instance within the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It is built on the x86_64 architecture, featuring a dedicated AMD EPYC processor with 24 physical cores and 48 virtual CPUs running at a base speed of 2.0 GHz. The hardware configuration includes 384.0 GB of system memory, providing a resource density of 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Storage is bundled with 2880 GB of local NVMe SSD capacity, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The CPU supports advanced instruction sets, including AVX-512 vector extensions, AVX-512 Vector Neural Network Instructions, and hardware-accelerated cryptography via AES and SHA extensions.

In benchmark evaluations, the server demonstrates strong multi-core and memory performance. The AMD EPYC processor achieves a stress-ng single-core CPU score of 3702.98, placing it in the top 10% tier, while its multi-core performance reaches 88688.86, ranking in the top 25%. Memory bandwidth is a notable strength, with large-block read-only speeds of 414.9 GB/sec and write speeds of 213.09 GB/sec, both scoring in the top 10% tier. Database operations and key-value store performance are also robust, as evidenced by a Passmark database score of 30834.1 and a Redis SET throughput of 85.37 million operations per second. For text processing and compression, the instance achieves a single-threaded gzip compression speed of 40.56 GB/sec.

Given its high memory-to-core ratio and dedicated CPU allocation, this instance offers high resource density for workloads requiring substantial RAM without necessitating GPU acceleration. The combination of 384.0 GB of RAM and 2880 GB of fast local NVMe SSD storage makes it highly cost-efficient for memory-intensive and data-heavy applications. It is well-suited for hosting large relational databases, in-memory data stores like Redis, data warehousing, and enterprise-grade web serving. Additionally, the CPU's AVX-512 capabilities support moderate machine learning tasks, such as small to medium LLM inference, where it achieves 38.84 tokens per second for text generation on a 7B parameter model.
